readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A truth universally acknowledged
readings.challenge: Reread the first sentence after finishing Chapter I and decide whose “truth” it really is. Austen often drops speech tags, so track who is speaking in each exchange.
readings.focus: Irony in the narrator’s generalization and in a marriage conducted as a contest of teasing and misreading.
readings.context: Pride and Prejudice (1813) is Jane Austen’s comedy of courtship among the landowning families of an English village; this text follows an 1894 London edition. The Bennets of Longbourn have five daughters and no son. Netherfield Park, a large house nearby, has just been rented (“let”). By custom the father of a family called on a newly arrived gentleman before his wife and daughters could be introduced to him. Four or five thousand pounds a year was a very large income; Michaelmas is September 29.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapters I and II, complete; opens “IT is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune…”; closes “…he would return Mr. Bennet’s visit, and determining when they should ask him to dinner.”.

questions.prompt: The first sentence calls a belief “universally acknowledged.” Whose belief does the second paragraph, and then Mrs. Bennet, show it to be?
facilitatorNotes: The second paragraph moves the “truth” into “the minds of the surrounding families,” who treat a wealthy newcomer as the “rightful property” of their daughters, while his own feelings are “little known.” Mrs. Bennet then acts it out. The irony is that a neighbourhood’s wish is dressed as a law of nature.

Some readers also hear a real economic truth reversed: the daughters need husbands more than the rich man needs a wife. Both readings depend on noticing that the sentence is not as neutral as it sounds.
evidence: he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters
However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be

questions.prompt: How does Mr. Bennet turn his wife’s words against her? Choose one reply and explain what makes it a joke at her expense.
facilitatorNotes: He answers her marriage plan with “Is that his design in settling here?”, treating her hope as Bingley’s intention, and he calls her nerves “my old friends.” He prefers provoking her to informing her.
Readers may find him witty, unkind, or both. The narrator’s summary of him as “so odd a mixture of quick parts, sarcastic humour, reserve, and caprice” supports more than one judgment.
evidence: Is that his design in settling here?
I have a high respect for your nerves. They are my old friends.

questions.prompt: In Chapter II Mr. Bennet reveals that he visited Bingley all along. Why does he hide it, and how does Mrs. Bennet rewrite the event once she knows?
facilitatorNotes: He stages a surprise for its effect: “The astonishment of the ladies was just what he wished.” She immediately claims she “had expected” it and credits her own persuasion. One partner performs; the other revises the record so her view stays intact.
Some students read the trick as affectionate; others notice that it works only because she is kept in ignorance.
evidence: The astonishment of the ladies was just what he wished
she began to declare that it was what she had expected all the while

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: The assembly at Meryton
readings.challenge: Follow how Darcy’s reputation changes within one evening, and separate what he actually says from what the room reports about him.
readings.focus: Public opinion forms quickly from income, manners and a single overheard remark.
readings.context: Recap: Mrs. Bennet hopes the wealthy newcomer Mr. Bingley will marry one of her five daughters, and Mr. Bennet, after teasing her, has called on him. An assembly is a public ball held in a town’s assembly rooms; partners “stood up” for two dances at a time. Darcy’s ten thousand a year makes him far richer than Bingley; Derbyshire is a county in the north Midlands.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter III, complete; opens “NOT all that Mrs. Bennet, however, with the assistance of her five daughters, could ask…”; closes “…been there, my dear, to have given him one of your set-downs. I quite detest the man.””.

questions.prompt: How long does it take the assembly to decide that Darcy is admirable, and then that he is not? Which words show the judgment shifting?
facilitatorNotes: His income is “in general circulation within five minutes”; he is admired “for about half the evening” until his manners turn “the tide of his popularity.” “His character was decided” reports the room’s verdict in the narrator’s voice, with irony: a whole character settled in one night.
Some readers think the verdict is fair, since he really does refuse to be introduced to anyone. The question is less whether he behaved badly than how much one evening can prove.
evidence: the report, which was in general circulation within five minutes after his entrance, of his having ten thousand a year
His character was decided.

questions.prompt: What exactly does Darcy say about Elizabeth, and what does she do with it? Why might it matter that she “told the story … with great spirit”?
facilitatorNotes: He calls her “tolerable” and refuses to “give consequence to young ladies who are slighted by other men.” She turns the insult into a comic story because she “delighted in anything ridiculous.”
Her laughter may show she is unhurt, or it may be a defence of wounded pride. Both readings are available; the novel’s title invites readers to keep the question open.
evidence: She is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt me
She told the story, however, with great spirit among her friends

questions.prompt: Compare Mrs. Bennet’s report of the ball with the narrator’s account. What does she include, exaggerate or leave out?
facilitatorNotes: She counts Bingley’s partners in exhausting detail, dismisses Charlotte (“nobody can” admire her), and tells of Darcy’s rudeness “with much bitterness of spirit, and some exaggeration.” Mr. Bennet’s interruptions show his impatience with her way of telling.
The chapter trains readers to set a character’s version beside the narrator’s. Students may also notice that her anger at Darcy is the loyal reaction of a mother, however overstated.
evidence: related, with much bitterness of spirit, and some exaggeration, the shocking rudeness of Mr. Darcy
he did not admire her at all; indeed, nobody can, you know

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Two sisters, and a debate about pride
readings.challenge: Slow down for the long narrative paragraphs about the Bingleys and Darcy, which give information no character has. Then sort the different definitions of pride offered during the Lucases’ visit.
readings.focus: Jane’s generosity and Elizabeth’s quickness as two ways of judging people; pride distinguished from vanity.
readings.context: Recap: At the Meryton assembly Bingley danced twice with Jane, the eldest Bennet sister, while Darcy refused to dance with Elizabeth, calling her only “tolerable,” and the neighbourhood decided he was proud. “Candour” here means generosity in judging others. A fortune “acquired by trade” (commerce) ranked below inherited land. Sir William Lucas was knighted after presenting an address to the king at St. James’s Palace. A hack chaise is a hired carriage.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapters IV and V, complete; opens “WHEN Jane and Elizabeth were alone, the former, who had been cautious in her praise of…”; closes “…not; she continued to declare that she would; and the argument ended only with the visit.”.

questions.prompt: Elizabeth praises Jane for being “candid without ostentation or design.” What does she admire, and what does she think it costs Jane?
facilitatorNotes: Jane takes “the good of everybody’s character” and says nothing of the bad. Elizabeth admires the honesty of it but calls her sister “honestly blind” to others’ follies, so the praise carries a warning.
Readers may side with Jane, whose charity the novel does not simply dismiss, or with Elizabeth, whose sharper judgment the narrator credits with “more quickness of observation.”
evidence: With your good sense, to be so honestly blind to the follies and nonsense of others!
to be candid without ostentation or design

questions.prompt: The narrator says the Bingley sisters were “in every respect entitled to think well of themselves and meanly of others.” Is the narrator agreeing with them? Use the reasons listed and the clause that follows.
facilitatorNotes: The “therefore” rests their entitlement on a fashionable school, money, overspending and rank, none of which is a virtue, so the sentence is ironic. The next clause exposes what they prefer to forget: their fortune “had been acquired by trade.”
The narrator here knows more than Elizabeth does, which lets the reader test her quick judgment against fuller information.
evidence: were, therefore, in every respect entitled to think well of themselves and meanly of others
a circumstance more deeply impressed on their memories than that their brother’s fortune and their own had been acquired by trade

questions.prompt: Charlotte, Elizabeth, Mary and young Lucas each comment on Darcy’s pride. Whose view is most convincing, and whose is most self-revealing?
facilitatorNotes: Charlotte says his advantages give him “a right to be proud”; Elizabeth would forgive his pride “if he had not mortified mine”; Mary distinguishes pride from vanity; the boy wants foxhounds and wine. Elizabeth’s joke admits a wounded pride of her own, and Mary’s sound distinction is delivered as display.
Encourage readers to apply Mary’s definitions to Darcy and to Elizabeth. Several answers are defensible if they rest on what each speaker reveals.
evidence: I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine
Pride relates more to our opinion of ourselves; vanity to what we would have others think of us.

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Charlotte’s advice and a pair of fine eyes
readings.challenge: Treat Charlotte’s view of courtship as an argument rather than only a joke. Then notice how the narrator shows Darcy’s changing opinion while Elizabeth sees none of it.
readings.focus: Strategy and feeling in courtship, and the dramatic irony of a reader who knows what Elizabeth does not.
readings.context: Pride and Prejudice (1813) is Jane Austen’s comedy of courtship among the landowning families of an English village; this text follows an 1894 London edition. Elizabeth Bennet, the second of five daughters, was slighted at a ball by the proud and wealthy Mr. Darcy, while his friend Mr. Bingley admired her elder sister Jane. Charlotte Lucas, twenty-seven, is Elizabeth’s closest friend. Vingt-un and Commerce are card games; to “fix” a man is to secure his proposal; St. James’s is the royal court.
readings.contentNote: Darcy’s retort that “every savage can dance” uses a period slur for non-European peoples; it belongs to his voice and his era.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter VI, complete; opens “THE ladies of Longbourn soon waited on those of Netherfield. The visit was returned in…”; closes “…this manner; and as his composure convinced her that all was safe, her wit flowed along.”.

questions.prompt: Charlotte claims that “Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.” Reconstruct her reasoning. Is Elizabeth right that it “is not sound”?
facilitatorNotes: Charlotte argues that affection needs encouragement, that married people grow unlike anyway, and that it is better to know little of a partner’s defects. Elizabeth laughs and insists Charlotte would never act on it herself.

Given how few choices women in Charlotte’s position had, her reasoning is coherent, and some readers find her more realistic than Elizabeth. Keep Elizabeth’s confident prediction in mind as the novel continues.
evidence: Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.
You know it is not sound, and that you would never act in this way yourself.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator report Darcy’s growing interest? Which words show that each discovery happens against his will?
facilitatorNotes: He first finds “hardly a good feature,” then eyes made “uncommonly intelligent”; he is “forced to acknowledge” her figure and “caught by” her playfulness. Each discovery is “mortifying” because it contradicts what he has already declared.
The paragraph ends inside Elizabeth’s view of him, so readers know more than she does, a pattern Austen uses throughout.
evidence: To this discovery succeeded some others equally mortifying.
to her he was only the man who made himself agreeable nowhere

questions.prompt: Darcy says a lady’s imagination “jumps from admiration to love, from love to matrimony, in a moment.” Does Miss Bingley prove him right? What does her teasing reveal?
facilitatorNotes: She leaps at once to “when am I to wish you joy?” and mocks a future “charming mother-in-law,” so she seems to prove his point. Yet her wit flows only once she is sure “all was safe,” which suggests the teasing covers anxiety about her own hopes of Darcy.
Some readers note that Darcy’s generalization about women is itself condescending, even when one woman fits it.
evidence: it jumps from admiration to love, from love to matrimony, in a moment
as his composure convinced her that all was safe, her wit flowed along

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Rain, a note and a three-mile walk
readings.challenge: Read the opening paragraphs about money as the background for every later choice. Then compare how each member of the family responds to news of Jane’s illness.
readings.focus: Economic facts beneath the comedy, and Elizabeth’s walk as a choice that others read differently.
readings.context: Recap: Charlotte Lucas argued that Jane should show Bingley more affection to secure him, and Darcy, unseen by Elizabeth, has begun to admire her “fine eyes.” An estate “entailed, in default of heirs male” must pass to the nearest male relative, so the Bennet daughters will not inherit their father’s land. A militia regiment was a home-defence force, here quartered in Meryton for the winter; an ensign was the most junior officer. Mr. Jones, an apothecary, was the local medical practitioner.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter VII, complete; opens “MR. BENNET’S property consisted almost entirely in an estate of two thousand a year,…”; closes “…to Longbourn, to acquaint the family with her stay, and bring back a supply of clothes.”.

questions.prompt: What do the first two paragraphs tell you about the Bennets’ money and connections? How do those facts change the way you read Mrs. Bennet’s schemes?
facilitatorNotes: The estate is entailed away from the daughters, and their mother’s four thousand pounds “could but ill supply the deficiency.” Her urgency about marriage has a material cause even when it is comic.
Her relatives in law and trade also prepare for later sneers about the family’s connections. Students may still judge her methods foolish while recognizing the pressure behind them.
evidence: entailed, in default of heirs male, on a distant relation
could but ill supply the deficiency of his

questions.prompt: Mrs. Bennet sends Jane on horseback and is pleased when it rains. How do the narrator and Mr. Bennet each judge her plan?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator mocks her: she speaks “as if the credit of making it rain were all her own.” Mr. Bennet’s grim joke, that if Jane died it would be “in pursuit of Mr. Bingley, and under your orders,” points to a real risk under the comedy.
Some readers hear his remark as a fair rebuke; others hear a father who mocks rather than intervenes.
evidence: as if the credit of making it rain were all her own
it would be a comfort to know that it was all in pursuit of Mr. Bingley, and under your orders

questions.prompt: Elizabeth arrives with “dirty stockings, and a face glowing.” How do the people at Netherfield read her appearance, and what do their readings reveal about them?
facilitatorNotes: The sisters find the walk “almost incredible” and hold her in contempt; Bingley shows “good-humour and kindness”; Darcy is divided between admiration and doubt about her coming “so far alone”; Mr. Hurst thinks of breakfast. One sight, several judgments, and each tells us about the viewer.
Mary’s maxim that exertion should be “in proportion to what is required” offers yet another frame; readers can decide whether Elizabeth’s walk was proportionate.
evidence: The former was divided between admiration of the brilliancy which exercise had given to her complexion and doubt as to the occasion’s justifying her coming so far alone.
The latter was thinking only of his breakfast.

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: The accomplished woman
readings.challenge: Listen for what each speaker gains from the judgments they make. In the argument about accomplishments, follow how the definition grows with each speaker.
readings.focus: Contempt disguised as concern, and a debate about what makes a woman “accomplished.”
readings.context: Recap: Jane fell ill at Netherfield after riding there in the rain, and Elizabeth walked three muddy miles to nurse her; Bingley’s sisters were scornful and Darcy admired her complexion. Cheapside was a commercial street in London, so an uncle living near it was in trade. Loo is a card game played for money. Pemberley is Darcy’s estate in Derbyshire. Netting purses and covering screens were genteel handicrafts.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter VIII, complete; opens “AT five o’clock the two ladies retired to dress, and at half-past six Elizabeth was…”; closes “…directions that every possible attention might be paid to the sick lady and her sister.”.

questions.prompt: When the sisters mock Elizabeth’s walk and laugh at the uncle near Cheapside, how do Bingley and Darcy answer? How do their answers differ?
facilitatorNotes: Bingley praises her affection for her sister and says uncles enough “to fill all Cheapside” would not make the Bennets less agreeable. Darcy says such connections lessen their chance of marrying “men of any consideration.” Bingley judges character; Darcy states a social fact, coldly and perhaps accurately.
Some readers think Darcy is only describing the world; others hear him endorsing its snobbery. His earlier admiration of her eyes complicates either view.
evidence: If they had uncles enough to fill all Cheapside
it must very materially lessen their chance of marrying men of any consideration in the world

questions.prompt: Trace how the definition of an “accomplished” woman grows from Bingley to Miss Bingley to Darcy. What is Elizabeth’s reply really saying?
facilitatorNotes: Bingley thinks every young lady is accomplished; Miss Bingley adds music, languages and “a certain something” in manner; Darcy adds “extensive reading.” Elizabeth replies that she never saw such a woman: the ideal is impossible, and the list says more about the speakers than about women.
Some readers notice that Darcy’s addition describes the one person in the room who chose a book over cards. Others find his standard as unreal as Miss Bingley’s.
evidence: and to all she must yet add something more substantial in the improvement of her mind by extensive reading
I never saw such capacity, and taste, and application, and elegance, as you describe, united.

questions.prompt: Miss Bingley calls Elizabeth’s manner “a paltry device.” How does Darcy’s reply turn the charge back on Miss Bingley?
facilitatorNotes: He condemns “all the arts which ladies sometimes condescend to employ for captivation.” Her flattery of Pemberley and praise of his sister are exactly such arts, which is why she is “not so entirely satisfied” and drops the subject.
Students might also question Darcy’s sweeping statement about “ladies,” which is as much a generalization as hers.
evidence: there is meanness in all the arts which ladies sometimes condescend to employ for captivation
Miss Bingley was not so entirely satisfied with this reply as to continue the subject.

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Mrs. Bennet at Netherfield
readings.challenge: Compare what the narrator tells you about Mrs. Bennet’s motives with what she says aloud. In the quarrel about the country, work out what Darcy meant and what Mrs. Bennet heard.
readings.focus: A mother’s visit turns a sickroom into a stage for matchmaking, and Elizabeth must defend Darcy’s meaning against her own family.
readings.context: Pride and Prejudice (1813) is Jane Austen’s comedy of courtship among the landowning families of an English village; this text follows an 1894 London edition. Recap: Jane fell ill while visiting Netherfield, Mr. Bingley’s rented house, and Elizabeth walked three miles to nurse her, to the scorn of Bingley’s sisters. Mr. Jones is the local apothecary, a medical man below the rank of physician. A girl was “brought into public” when she began attending balls and dinners as a grown woman; most families waited until a daughter was older than fifteen. Captain Carter and Colonel Forster are officers of a militia regiment stationed at Meryton for the winter. To “tax” someone here means to challenge him with something.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter IX, complete; opens “ELIZABETH passed the chief of the night in her sister’s room, and in the morning had the…”; closes “…to join in their censure of her, in spite of all Miss Bingley’s witticisms on fine eyes.”.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Bennet tells Bingley that Jane is “a great deal too ill to be moved.” What has the narrator already told you that Bingley does not know?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator reports that Mrs. Bennet was “satisfied on seeing her that her illness was not alarming” and did not want her to recover quickly, because recovery would send her home from Netherfield. Her speech to Bingley is a performance aimed at keeping Jane near him.

Students may say she still loves Jane, and her praise of Jane’s “sweetest temper” can be sincere. The irony is that her love is expressed as strategy: the daughter’s comfort matters less than the daughter’s chances.
evidence: she had no wish of her recovering immediately, as her restoration to health would probably remove her from Netherfield
She is a great deal too ill to be moved.

questions.prompt: Darcy says country society is “confined and unvarying.” How does Mrs. Bennet hear the remark, and why does her answer about “four-and-twenty families” prove his point rather than hers?
facilitatorNotes: Darcy means that a village offers few new kinds of people; Mrs. Bennet hears an insult to the country and believes she has “gained a complete victory.” Boasting that the family dines with twenty-four households shows exactly how small the circle is, which is why Bingley can barely “keep his countenance” and Miss Bingley smiles at Darcy.

Elizabeth, “blushing for her mother,” explains Darcy’s meaning against her own family. Some readers also find Darcy’s remark condescending, so Mrs. Bennet’s offence is not baseless even if her reply is absurd.
evidence: In a country neighbourhood you move in a very confined and unvarying society.
I know we dine with four-and-twenty families.
Elizabeth, blushing for her mother

questions.prompt: Elizabeth jokes that poetry drives love away, and Darcy calls poetry “the food of love.” Why does she make the joke at this moment, and what does her reply say about strong and weak feelings?
facilitatorNotes: She interrupts her mother’s story about the gentleman who wrote verses on Jane, turning an embarrassing boast into a general witticism. Her reply argues that writing about love only feeds a “fine, stout, healthy love” but finishes off a “slight, thin sort of inclination.”

Darcy’s line echoes a familiar idea (Shakespeare opens Twelfth Night with “If music be the food of love”). Some readers hear the start of a real debate between the two; others see Elizabeth simply rescuing the family from another exposure, since she is soon trembling “lest her mother should be exposing herself again.”
evidence: I wonder who first discovered the efficacy of poetry in driving away love!
I have been used to consider poetry as the food of love
one good sonnet will starve it entirely away

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A letter, a reel and the picturesque
readings.challenge: Follow a long argument that changes its subject: from writing letters, to modesty, to whether a friend should yield to persuasion. Then notice where the narrator lets you into Darcy’s thoughts.
readings.focus: Elizabeth and Darcy argue on principle while the narrator shows what neither knows about the other.
readings.context: Recap: Mrs. Bennet visited Netherfield and quarrelled with Darcy about country society, and Lydia made Bingley promise to give a ball. Jane is slowly recovering. Piquet is a card game for two players. A quill pen had to be “mended,” cut to a fresh point with a penknife. A reel is a lively Scottish dance. The “picturesque” was a fashionable taste for scenery and groups arranged as if for a painting.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter X, complete; opens “THE day passed much as the day before had done. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley had spent…”; closes “…so much recovered as to intend leaving her room for a couple of hours that evening.”.

questions.prompt: In the letter-writing scene Miss Bingley speaks and Darcy replies. What pattern do their exchanges follow, and what does it show about each of them?
facilitatorNotes: She praises everything about his letter, often inaccurately (“You write uncommonly fast”), and he corrects, deflects or stays silent. Elizabeth enjoys the “curious dialogue” because it confirms her opinion of both: one flatters, the other receives flattery with “perfect unconcern.”
Some readers find Darcy rude; others think he is simply refusing to be flattered. Either way, the scene shows that Miss Bingley’s method of pleasing him does not work.
evidence: You write uncommonly fast.
You are mistaken. I write rather slowly.
the perfect unconcern with which her praises were received

questions.prompt: Darcy calls Bingley’s modesty “an indirect boast,” and the argument moves to whether one should yield to a friend’s request. What does each of them value?
facilitatorNotes: Darcy values reason and consistency: “To yield without conviction is no compliment to the understanding of either.” Elizabeth values affection: a friend may comply “without waiting to be argued into it.” Bingley, the subject of the argument, prefers to stop it.

Students can take either side; both positions have costs. It is worth remembering how quickly, according to Darcy, Bingley could be talked into staying or going, because the novel returns to how easily he is persuaded.
evidence: Nothing is more deceitful,” said Darcy, “than the appearance of humility.
To yield without conviction is no compliment to the understanding of either.
You appear to me, Mr. Darcy, to allow nothing for the influence of friendship and affection.

questions.prompt: Elizabeth decides that Darcy looks at her because he finds her “more wrong and reprehensible” than anyone else. What does the narrator tell you that she does not know?
facilitatorNotes: After she refuses the reel, the narrator enters Darcy’s mind: he had “never been so bewitched by any woman,” and only the “inferiority of her connections” keeps him safe. Elizabeth’s interpretation fits her low opinion of him, not the evidence; the reader now knows more than the heroine.
Some readers see her reading as reasonable, given his first insult at the assembly. Others notice that she has made up her mind and fits each new glance to it.
evidence: she drew his notice because there was something about her more wrong and reprehensible, according to his ideas of right, than in any other person present
Darcy had never been so bewitched by any woman as he was by her
were it not for the inferiority of her connections, he should be in some danger

questions.prompt: In the shrubbery Miss Bingley mocks Elizabeth’s relations, and Mrs. Hurst then leaves Elizabeth to walk alone. How does Elizabeth turn the slight into a joke at their expense?
facilitatorNotes: Miss Bingley suggests hanging the Philipses, a country attorney and his wife, beside Darcy’s great-uncle the judge, a sneer at the Bennets’ connections in trade and law. Mrs. Hurst then takes Darcy’s free arm on a path that “just admitted three.” Elizabeth refuses Darcy’s offer to move and calls the three of them “charmingly grouped,” as if they were a picture that a fourth figure would spoil.
Her laughter lets her leave on her own terms. Some readers hear real hurt beneath the wit; Darcy, at least, “felt their rudeness.”
evidence: Do let the portraits of your uncle and aunt Philips be placed in the gallery at Pemberley.
You are charmingly grouped, and appear to uncommon advantage.
Mr. Darcy felt their rudeness

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A turn about the room
readings.challenge: Watch how characters use reading, walking and music to attract or avoid attention. In the argument about faults, decide how far each speaker’s charge against the other is fair.
readings.focus: Darcy and Elizabeth name each other’s defects, and the visit to Netherfield ends.
readings.context: Recap: at Netherfield Darcy and Elizabeth argued about whether yielding to a friend is a virtue, she refused to dance a reel with him, and the narrator revealed that he is attracted to her despite her family. Miss Bingley, jealous, mocks the Bennets. White soup was a rich dish served at balls; Bingley will “send round” printed invitation cards. Thorough bass is the theory of musical harmony. The officers belong to the militia regiment in Meryton.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapters XI and XII, complete; opens “WHEN the ladies removed after dinner Elizabeth ran up to her sister, and seeing her well…”; closes “…flogged; and it had actually been hinted that Colonel Forster was going to be married.”.

questions.prompt: Miss Bingley declares that “there is no enjoyment like reading.” What has the narrator already told you about her book?
facilitatorNotes: She chose it “only” because it was the second volume of Darcy’s, she watches his page more than her own, and she yawns before and after her praise of reading. Her speech is aimed at Darcy, who was praised in Chapter VIII for adding “extensive reading” to the accomplished woman.
The comedy depends on the narrator giving the motive first, so readers hear her line as a performance. Some may feel sympathy for a woman so plainly failing to be noticed.
evidence: which she had only chosen because it was the second volume of his
I declare, after all, there is no enjoyment like reading!

questions.prompt: Darcy says he has studied to avoid weaknesses that expose a strong mind to ridicule. When Elizabeth says “Such as vanity and pride,” how does he separate the two, and why does she turn away “to hide a smile”?
facilitatorNotes: He grants that vanity is a weakness but says pride, “where there is a real superiority of mind,” will be “under good regulation.” Elizabeth smiles because the claim itself sounds proud: he assumes his own superiority while defending it.
Some readers think Darcy is making a fair distinction between self-respect and showing off. The novel’s title keeps the question open.
evidence: Such as vanity and pride.
pride—where there is a real superiority of mind—pride will be always under good regulation
Elizabeth turned away to hide a smile.

questions.prompt: Darcy calls his own temper resentful, and the two end by naming each other’s “defect.” What does each accuse the other of, and which charge do you find more accurate so far?
facilitatorNotes: Darcy admits that his “good opinion once lost is lost for ever.” Elizabeth sums this up as “a propensity to hate everybody”; he answers that her defect is “wilfully to misunderstand them.” Each charge exaggerates, but each touches something the reader has seen: Darcy’s unbending judgments, and Elizabeth’s readiness to read his looks as contempt.
Accept either answer with evidence from earlier chapters. The exchange ends with a smile, which suggests both are enjoying the contest.
evidence: My good opinion once lost is lost for ever.
And your defect is a propensity to hate everybody.
And yours,” he replied, with a smile, “is wilfully to misunderstand them.

questions.prompt: In Chapter XII Darcy decides to show no “sign of admiration” on the last day. What does his reasoning assume about Elizabeth, and what do we know that he does not?
facilitatorNotes: He fears she might be encouraged in “the hope of influencing his felicity,” that is, of marrying him. He assumes she wants his attention, while the reader knows she “liked him too little to care for his approbation.” His careful silence is wasted on someone who is not waiting for it.
Students may also notice the contrast with Kitty and Lydia’s news from the regiment, where a flogging is listed beside a rumoured marriage, as if both were equally good gossip.
evidence: nothing that could elevate her with the hope of influencing his felicity
he adhered most conscientiously to his book, and would not even look at her
a private had been flogged; and it had actually been hinted that Colonel Forster was going to be married

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: The Gardiners come for Christmas
readings.challenge: Compare how Mrs. Bennet, Elizabeth and Mrs. Gardiner explain the same disappointment, and notice the places where the narrator quietly corrects a speaker.
readings.focus: A sensible aunt from outside the family’s quarrels tests both Mrs. Bennet’s grievances and Elizabeth’s certainties, while her own memory bends to fit a story she has just heard.
readings.context: Pride and Prejudice (1813) is Jane Austen’s comedy of courtship among the landowning families of an English village; this text follows an 1894 London edition. By this point Elizabeth has refused a proposal from her cousin Mr. Collins, the clergyman who will inherit Longbourn because the estate is entailed on the male line, and within days he became engaged to her friend Charlotte Lucas instead. Mr. Bingley, who seemed in love with Jane, has gone to London, and his sister Caroline has written that he will not return; Elizabeth blames his friend Mr. Darcy. Mr. Wickham, a charming officer, has told Elizabeth that Darcy cheated him of a church living that Darcy’s father meant him to have. Mrs. Bennet’s brother, Mr. Gardiner, is a London merchant who lives in Gracechurch Street, near his warehouses in the commercial City of London, far from the fashionable streets where the Bingleys stay.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXV, complete; opens “AFTER a week spent in professions of love and schemes of felicity, Mr. Collins was called…”; closes “…having heard Mr. Fitzwilliam Darcy formerly spoken of as a very proud, ill-natured boy.”.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator introduce Mr. Gardiner? What does the sentence about “the Netherfield ladies” suggest about their idea of people in trade?
facilitatorNotes: He is “sensible, gentlemanlike” and “greatly superior to his sister, as well by nature as education.” The narrator imagines Bingley’s sisters unable to believe that a man living “within view of his own warehouses” could be well-bred: the joke is on their snobbery, not on him.
Readers who remember Chapter IV may add that the Bingleys’ own fortune came from trade, which makes the sisters’ contempt sharper. The point stands without that detail.
evidence: Mr. Gardiner was a sensible, gentlemanlike man, greatly superior to his sister, as well by nature as education.
a man who lived by trade, and within view of his own warehouses, could have been so well-bred and agreeable

questions.prompt: Mrs. Bennet blames Elizabeth’s “perverseness” and the Lucases’ selfishness in one breath. How does the narration make her grievance comic, and is there anything real underneath it?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator repeats her complaint in her own exaggerated terms (“They had all been very ill-used”), and her speech accuses the Lucases of thinking of themselves while she thinks only of her own family. It ends by swerving to the news of “long sleeves,” which deflates everything before it.
Underneath the comedy the worry is real: with the estate “just as much entailed as ever,” her daughters may have no home when Mr. Bennet dies. Students can hold both readings.
evidence: They had all been very ill-used since she last saw her sister.
Longbourn estate is just as much entailed as ever
I am very glad to hear what you tell us of long sleeves

questions.prompt: Mrs. Gardiner doubts the phrase “violently in love.” What evidence does Elizabeth give that Bingley really loved Jane, and how certain is she, according to the narrator, that he is gone for good?
facilitatorNotes: She offers symptoms: he neglected other people, offended young ladies by not dancing with them, and twice failed to answer Elizabeth herself. Her question “Is not general incivility the very essence of love?” is a joke that still makes a serious point.

She tells her aunt a meeting is “quite impossible,” but the narrator says she only “affected” that certainty and privately thought renewed affection “possible, and sometimes … probable.” Ask why someone might speak more certainly than she feels: to protect Jane, or herself, from hope.
evidence: that expression of ‘violently in love’ is so hackneyed, so doubtful, so indefinite
Is not general incivility the very essence of love?
in spite of the certainty in which Elizabeth affected to place this point

questions.prompt: Read the last sentence closely. How does Mrs. Gardiner arrive at her memory of young Darcy, and what does the order of the sentence suggest about how reliable that memory is?
facilitatorNotes: She hears Wickham’s account first, then “tried to remember something … which might agree with it,” and only “at last” becomes “confident” that she heard Darcy called a proud, ill-natured boy. The memory is searched for to fit a story, not recalled on its own.
This does not prove the memory false; it shows how testimony can be shaped by what a listener already believes. Students may connect it with how quickly Meryton judged Darcy at the first ball.
evidence: she tried to remember something of that gentleman’s reputed disposition, when quite a lad, which might agree with it
was confident, at last, that she recollected having heard Mr. Fitzwilliam Darcy formerly spoken of as a very proud, ill-natured boy

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: A caution, a wedding and a letter from London
readings.challenge: Weigh three kinds of evidence, an aunt’s warning, Charlotte’s letters and Jane’s long letter, and ask of each what it leaves unsaid.
readings.focus: Elizabeth reads other people’s letters shrewdly, yet the narrator shows her excusing in Wickham the kind of prudent marriage she condemned in Charlotte.
readings.context: Recap: Mrs. Gardiner, Elizabeth’s sensible aunt from London, has spent Christmas at Longbourn, invited Jane to stay with her in town, and noticed how much Elizabeth likes Mr. Wickham. Charlotte Lucas is about to marry Mr. Collins, whose parsonage is at Hunsford in Kent, beside Rosings, the great house of his patroness Lady Catherine de Bourgh. Caroline Bingley is Mr. Bingley’s sister; Miss Darcy is Mr. Darcy’s younger sister. Miss King, a young woman of the neighbourhood, has just inherited ten thousand pounds.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXVI, complete; opens “MRS. GARDINER’S caution to Elizabeth was punctually and kindly given on the first…”; closes “…conviction that handsome young men must have something to live on as well as the plain.””.

questions.prompt: Elizabeth answers her aunt’s warning first with a joke and then “seriously.” What does her second answer promise, and what does it refuse to promise?
facilitatorNotes: She promises only “not to be in a hurry”: not to believe herself Wickham’s first object and not to be “wishing.” She will not promise to resist an attachment, because she sees young people marry without fortune “every day” and asks how she can be “wiser” than they are.

Some readers find the answer honest; others hear her keeping a door open. The narrator’s comment, “a wonderful instance of advice being given on such a point without being resented,” is gently ironic about how rare her calm response is.
evidence: All that I can promise you, therefore, is not to be in a hurry.
how can I promise to be wiser than so many of my fellow-creatures, if I am tempted
a wonderful instance of advice being given on such a point without being resented

questions.prompt: Why can Elizabeth’s letters with Charlotte no longer be “unreserved”? What does she notice about Charlotte’s cheerful reports from Hunsford?
facilitatorNotes: Charlotte has married a man Elizabeth thinks foolish, so “all the comfort of intimacy was over.” Charlotte’s letters praise everything and mention “nothing which she could not praise”; Elizabeth reads them as Mr. Collins’s boasting “rationally softened” and decides she must see for herself.
Students may argue that Charlotte is simply content and Elizabeth is reading in a disappointment that is not there. The chapter gives grounds for both, which is why Elizabeth waits for her visit.
evidence: that it should be equally unreserved was impossible
mentioned nothing which she could not praise
It was Mr. Collins’s picture of Hunsford and Rosings rationally softened

questions.prompt: Jane’s long letter admits that she was deceived. Where does she come closest to accusing Caroline Bingley, and how does she soften the accusation?
facilitatorNotes: “A strong appearance of duplicity” is her harshest phrase, and even it is wrapped in conditions: “If I were not afraid of judging harshly, I should be almost tempted to say.” She also excuses Caroline as anxious for her brother and defends her own trust as “as natural as your suspicion.”
Readers may admire Jane’s fairness or find it painful self-deception. Note that she still refuses to blame Bingley himself: “if he had at all cared about me, we must have met long, long ago.”
evidence: If I were not afraid of judging harshly, I should be almost tempted to say, that there is a strong appearance of duplicity in all this.
my confidence was as natural as your suspicion
if he had at all cared about me, we must have met long, long ago

questions.prompt: Elizabeth was disgusted when Charlotte married for security, yet she does not “quarrel with” Wickham for courting an heiress. What does the narrator signal with the words “less clear-sighted perhaps in this case than in Charlotte’s”?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator points out an inconsistency Elizabeth does not see: she forgives in a man she likes the same prudence she condemned in her friend. Her own explanation, that her heart was “but slightly touched” and her “vanity was satisfied,” suggests feeling is shaping her judgment.

A defensible alternative: Elizabeth’s reasoning is consistent, since she accepts that people without money must marry with money in mind, and her bitter last line about young men who “must have something to live on” applies to both cases. The word “perhaps” leaves room for this debate.
evidence: less clear-sighted perhaps in this case than in Charlotte’s, did not quarrel with him for his wish of independence
her vanity was satisfied with believing that she would have been his only choice, had fortune permitted it
handsome young men must have something to live on as well as the plain

readings.title: Pride and Prejudice excerpt: Mercenary or prudent?
readings.challenge: Follow the quick exchange between Elizabeth and her aunt, in which many speeches have no speaker named, and decide who has the better of each turn.
readings.focus: Elizabeth tries to erase the line between prudence and greed, and her aunt hears disappointment under the wit.
readings.context: Recap: Jane is staying with the Gardiners in London and has learned that Caroline Bingley wants nothing more to do with her. Mr. Wickham has turned his attentions from Elizabeth to Miss King, who has just inherited ten thousand pounds, and Elizabeth has written to her aunt that she was never much in love. Charlotte, now Mrs. Collins, has asked Elizabeth to visit her in Kent with Charlotte’s father, Sir William Lucas, and her sister Maria. A chaise is a hired travelling carriage; the Lakes are the Lake District of northern England, admired for its mountains and lakes.

excerpt.locator: Pride and Prejudice, Chapter XXVII, complete; opens “WITH no greater events than these in the Longbourn family, and otherwise diversified by…”; closes “…our first effusions be less insupportable than those of the generality of travellers.””.

questions.prompt: Elizabeth had not at first thought seriously of going to Hunsford. What reasons does the first paragraph give for her change of mind, and which seems strongest?
facilitatorNotes: Absence has made her miss Charlotte and “weakened her disgust of Mr. Collins”; the trip is a novelty; home, “with such a mother and such uncompanionable sisters,” is not faultless; and she can see Jane in London on the way.
Students can rank them differently. The phrase “a little change was not unwelcome for its own sake” suggests restlessness as much as friendship.
evidence: Absence had increased her desire of seeing Charlotte again, and weakened her disgust of Mr. Collins.
with such a mother and such uncompanionable sisters, home could not be faultless

questions.prompt: Reread the long sentence about Elizabeth’s farewell to Wickham. Whose view of him does it give, and what makes its last words sound ironic to a careful reader?
facilitatorNotes: It reports Elizabeth’s feelings in the narrator’s voice: the repeated “the first” lists everything that flatters her, and she leaves “convinced” he “must always be her model of the amiable and pleasing.” The word “convinced” and the grand “always” invite the reader to doubt a judgment built on being admired.
Some readers take the sentence at face value, as a friendly parting. Ask what Wickham has actually done in the last two chapters, and whether being pleasing is the same as being good.
evidence: the first to excite and to deserve his attention, the first to listen and to pity, the first to be admired
she parted from him convinced, that, whether married or single, he must always be her model of the amiable and pleasing

questions.prompt: Elizabeth asks, “Where does discretion end, and avarice begin?” How does she turn her aunt’s own warning against her, and does she win the argument?
facilitatorNotes: She points out that last Christmas her aunt thought a marriage between Elizabeth and Wickham “imprudent” because neither had money, so his pursuit of a richer girl is only the prudence the aunt recommended. Mrs. Gardiner shifts ground to timing (“so soon after this event”) and to Miss King’s judgment.

Elizabeth’s last word, “He shall be mercenary, and she shall be foolish,” gives up the argument with sarcasm rather than winning it. Many readers think the aunt’s distinction between a motive and the indelicate way it is pursued is fair.
evidence: Where does discretion end, and avarice begin?
Last Christmas you were afraid of his marrying me, because it would be imprudent
He shall be mercenary, and she shall be foolish.

questions.prompt: Mrs. Gardiner says Elizabeth’s outburst against men “savours strongly of disappointment.” Read Elizabeth’s reply to the invitation to the Lakes. Has she recovered, or is she still disappointed?
facilitatorNotes: Her rapture (“What are men to rocks and mountains?”) can be read as relief and a real love of new scenes, or as the same disappointment turned into extravagance. Her earlier line, “Stupid men are the only ones worth knowing,” is plainly bitter.

Her plan to remember accurately what she sees, so that lakes and rivers are not “jumbled together,” also fits a heroine who prides herself on clear judgment. Accept either reading that uses both speeches.
evidence: Stupid men are the only ones worth knowing, after all.
that speech savours strongly of disappointment
What are men to rocks and mountains?
